line2_orientation: Dense, compact objects fall at similar speeds regardless of their specific shape; their exact impact times rely on specific environmental factors. Only lightweight, thin objects with high surface-area-to-mass ratios fall significantly slower due to air resistance.
Poured liquids always follow a curved (parabolic) downward trajectory and spread outward immediately upon impacting a surface.

Rolling strictly requires a curved contact patch with the surface. Objects with flat bases, irregular contact areas, or symmetry-breaking protrusions will not roll, regardless of their overall shape. Round objects roll continuously on slopes, but require an initial kinetic push to roll temporarily on flat surfaces.
Gravity alone does not break the equilibrium of a stable resting object; movement requires a specific external trigger (e.g., wind, bump, vibration).
When a supporting surface is tilted slowly and gradually, static friction keeps objects completely stationary until a specific angle threshold is exceeded.

Rapidly removing a bottom supporting object causes upper objects to drop vertically in place due to inertia. Slowly removing it causes the upper objects to slide or topple as support is gradually lost.

Buoyancy depends on overall average density. Objects with trapped internal air pockets will float, but physically altering the object to expose or remove those air pockets (e.g., by slicing or crushing) will cause it to sink.
Collisions involving either a rigid object hitting a soft/elastic surface, or an elastic object hitting a hard surface, will result in a bounce rather than a dead stop.
Wind-blown lightweight flexible materials (like fabric) do not float perfectly straight; they follow air currents and will wrap around or cling to physical obstacles in their path.
An obstacle's ability to stop a moving object depends entirely on their relative mass and speed. Light or small obstacles will not stop heavy or fast-moving objects and will simply be knocked aside.
Objects cannot balance or stand in orientations where their geometry and center of mass fail to form a stable equilibrium.
If the camera angle obscures the spatial relationship, trajectory path, or landing zone of a falling or moving object, the physical outcome must be evaluated as 'cannot be determined'.
Always assume the most direct, intuitive, and simple physical outcome for an action (e.g., gently pushed items slide, liquids spread) without over-analyzing for dramatic or extreme results.

The Elevation/Attention Rule: When individuals are described as looking at an elevated environmental feature, such as a fountain flowing from the top of rocks, or standing on a far bank looking across a deep space, their facial direction should strictly be classified as 'Upward' due to the upward gaze required.
The Wall-Mount Rule: A portrait, sign, or object hung on a wall that faces directly into the room is geometrically considered to be facing 'Away' from the wall itself.

The Stage Recording Rule: If a camera is set up on the side of a room (e.g., the left side) to record an event where the audience is facing forward toward a stage, the camera is typically facing 'Right' (or towards the center stage) to capture the profile of the event, rather than facing strictly forward.

The Handle Orientation Rule: If the handle of a tool (such as a spoon, pan, or mop) is pointing to or positioned on the LEFT side of the user's perspective or a reference object, it is ergonomically optimized to be picked up with the LEFT hand. If positioned on the RIGHT, it favors the RIGHT hand.

The Precision vs. Gross Motor Rule: A person's handedness (dominant hand) is most evident in actions requiring fine motor control and precision (e.g., scooping spice, writing, stirring, manipulating small objects). It is LEAST evident in gross motor actions, passive holding, or bilateral tasks (e.g., plugging a charger, placing a frame, simply holding a phone, or typing).

The Active Execution Rule: When interacting with an object like a kettle or a tool, the active execution movement (e.g., lifting, pouring, or scooping) is the primary indicator of handedness, rather than passive stabilization actions (e.g., merely holding the handle or placing a lid).

Positions described relative to the 'frame' or 'image boundaries', such as the center of the frame or the top of the image, refer exclusively to 2D Cartesian coordinates (X/Y axes) and must not be evaluated using 3D depth relative to the camera (Z axis).

When two objects differ simultaneously in their horizontal positioning and their depth relative to the camera, their spatial alignment relative to each other is strictly diagonal, regardless of whether their front planes are oriented parallel to the camera.

When assessing the closest or farthest depth of specific anatomical parts of a subject viewed in a side or diagonal profile, protruding extremities such as the nose, beak, or leading shoulder represent the extreme depth limits and supersede broader anatomical regions like the entire head or body.

In evaluating the greatest proximity to a specific subject, direct physical contact or visual overlap by foreground environmental elements, such as surrounding grass, leaves, or branches, often takes precedence over biologically attached body parts that are positioned further back in the 3D space.

The Euclidean distance between two objects within the scene cannot be accurately deduced merely by comparing their respective distances to the camera; objects sharing a direct structural baseline, such as being placed on the same table or identical shelving unit, possess greater proximity to each other than to isolated objects sharing a similar camera depth.

Separate where an object is located, where its front or arrow points, and the direction its face or surface normal points. A person to another person's right is not necessarily moving right. A sign's arrow direction differs from the direction its readable face looks toward; a traffic light faces along its lens axis, not along its position beside a sign.

Bind the named reference instance and its supplied compass heading first. Determine the target's heading relative to that reference using arrow tips, vehicle front versus rear, face and gaze, and ground-plane orientation. Do not assume picture up is north. Same direction preserves the reference heading; opposite direction reverses it. For genuine ground-plane quarter-turns, clockwise order is north, east, south, west. Facing north gives right east and left west; facing east gives right south and left north.

For two arrows known to lie in a common plane, opposite arrow-tip directions imply opposite headings. For signs on different faces of a post or differently oriented traffic lights, screen left and right alone do not establish an opposite or quarter-turn relation. Inspect their physical mounting and visible faces instead of automatically treating both cases alike.

Profile labels and pairwise perpendicularity statements are noisy estimates. A frontal face plus a side profile does not prove an exact 90-degree relation for every physical axis. The same left-pointing label assigned to two cars cannot override visible front/rear features showing that they travel in opposite directions.

For a clock laid on the ground, identify the real hour and minute hands and their relative angle before compass calibration. Rotate the entire dial and both hands together until the given hand matches its stated heading. Preserve the signed angular separation. Do not reset the hour hand to the nine marker for west while leaving the other hand in its original compass direction, and do not assume the twelve marker remains north.

Identify the actual hinge or vertex and the two specified rays or planes. Trace them from their common origin before estimating an angle. A diagonal image profile does not uniquely mean 45 degrees, and a pair of profile labels does not directly measure a hinge opening. Judge visible geometry rather than choose a typical installation or tool angle from memory.

Distinguish an acute gap, the supplementary obtuse opening and a reflex rotation. If two adjacent angles use opposite rays of the same straight line they sum to 180 degrees. For a leaning phone or backrest, identify the particular forward ground or seat ray requested; a backward-leaning upright member can form an obtuse opening with that forward ray. Do not always return its acute tilt or assume every seat/back angle is exactly 90 degrees.

For a compass, safety pin or other two-arm tool, trace the two arms from the joint and estimate their actual spread. No law makes an open drafting compass a right angle or an open safety pin a fixed standard angle. For an easel or tripod, the opening between two legs viewed from the side differs from the azimuthal spacing of feet around a vertical axis; the latter may be 120 degrees for three equally spaced feet without making the former 120 degrees.

For hinged covers, windows or cases, identify the hinge axis and compare the two surfaces on the relevant side of the hinge. Closed and fully unfolded positions have different opening angles; do not identify 180 degrees with closed by default. A vertical face and a surface lying on a table can form a right angle, so do not force every pictured cover to be fully flat.

For rotor blades, count actual blades or trace their visible roots around the hub before using 360/n for equal azimuthal spacing. Common models and a graph listing four directions do not prove four physical blades. Perspective foreshortens projected angles, so distinguish physical equal spacing from unequal apparent gaps.

A right angle between named objects can concern their spatial layout rather than their facing directions. Locate all specified references and test the two conditions together. Distance from a microphone to a body part is distance from that microphone, not camera depth; compare the whole displacement and requested body part.

Switch to the named observer's eye position and actual facing or gaze direction. Camera visibility alone does not prove visibility to a police officer, driver or reclining person. Objects behind that observer or blocked along the eye-to-object line may not be visible; being farther from the camera does not itself hide them. Missing observer nodes require looking at the observer in the image, not substituting the camera viewpoint.

An exact number visible to someone else cannot be obtained by merely counting all trees visible in the photograph when that person's visual field and occlusions are not established. Similarly, do not invent an unseen person or photographer's facial direction in an image containing only objects.

For a top view, inspect which rim, opening, central knob, handle and spout remain after the stated removal. A lidded round vessel can have an outer circular outline and a central smaller knob. A jug's asymmetric spout and curved handle may prevent a perfect circle-plus-rectangle description. Do not replace the particular pictured construction with a generic pot template or infer a physical shape solely from a perspective ellipse.

A straight approximately symmetric mop shaft can usually be gripped with either hand. Placement to the left of buckets does not make it inherently left-handed. Hand preference requires actual handed geometry, access constraints or a specified user pose; relative image position alone is insufficient.

Separate a child's balance from the stability of a fixed ladder or playhouse. A securely supported ladder can remain in place while the child leans beyond their own support and loses balance. For a magnifier tilted onto its round rim, curved edge contact may allow rolling if unsupported; this differs from laying its face and handle flat. Do not infer a flat contact merely because the notebook is flat.

For a route required to avoid collisions, assess the whole body's needed clearance and inspect the visible empty passage, including headroom under an open shelf. A narrow gap is not automatically collision-free. For transferring a sticker between curved surfaces, compare visible vertical extent and usable surface width in the specified alignment; sharing a frontal profile alone does not prove a perfect fit.

A calm flat water surface reflects a virtual image with mirror geometry and unchanged physical dimensions; tilt changes orientation and projection rather than physically lengthening the person. Ripples can distort the image. Camera-projected extent, physical height and symmetry about the water plane are different claims.

Shadow size depends on the light, object and receiving surface geometry, not solely camera distance or a vague instruction to move backward. With a point light and fixed parallel screen, magnification is light-to-screen distance divided by light-to-object distance. Translation under approximately parallel illumination on the same receiving plane can preserve shadow scale. Do not infer smaller shadows just because the objects move farther from the camera.

Changing lamp position can enlarge, shorten or redirect a shadow depending on the new distances and angles. It does not physically grow the plant. A statement that a distant object appears smaller does not establish that its shadow becomes physically longer or invisible. Validate both parts of a compound option independently. Likewise moving a boat toward the camera does not universally shrink its reflection.

Treat precomputed geometry as auxiliary evidence and keep the question's reference and conditions explicit. A compass heading cannot be uniquely recovered from left/right placement without an absolute anchor. When an uncertainty option is available and essential information is missing, use it rather than invent a compass, measurement or exact observer field of view.

Separate object location, body orientation, gaze, motion and the particular part's pointing direction. Behind a figure describes its position, not an opposite or sideways heading. Two figures placed one behind another may face the same way. Decide from their faces, beaks, fronts or defining parts rather than the relative location alone.

Read explicit compass text and associate it with its own arrow or route panel before inventing a map from picture axes. A visible EAST or WEST route label calibrates the corresponding signed route direction. Another arrow aligned with that same road direction can inherit the calibration. Picture right is not automatically east and picture up is not automatically north.

For pencils, follow the actual sharpened tip; a decorative bent shaft can rise vertically and then point sideways. Do not use a graph's left/right label when the visible tip disagrees. Calibrate the reference tip to its given compass heading and preserve the signed angle to the target tip. For genuine ground-plane rotations, clockwise compass order is north, east, south, west; opposite reverses the heading.

For chairs, facing runs from backrest toward the open front of the seat. Different image profiles or opposite screen positions do not prove that the chairs face each other. A pair placed around adjacent sides of a table may form a quarter turn. Use seat fronts and backrests to distinguish that from opposite seating.

For a bus doorway or sign face, distinguish an outward surface normal from the vehicle's travel axis and from an arrow printed on the surface. For boats and cars on crossing waterways and roads, identify the correct instance and actual nose first. Side-profile labels alone do not establish parallel motion.

A scene-graph name that already claims north-facing or south-facing is an estimate, not an independent compass measurement. Verify it against the stated reference and the visible mounting. Do not derive compass headings from an uncalibrated forward, sideways or left-corner description.

Locate the hinge, vertex or baseline and the two rays defining the requested angle. A car door opens about its hinge relative to its closed plane, not relative to the camera's picture border. A monitor's tilt commonly means its small deviation from upright, whereas its angle to the desktop uses a different baseline. Choose the quantity asked for before comparing options.

A lamp has several distinct angles: its stem joint, the lamp-head axis, and the direction of emitted light. Trace the specified members; a vertical stem does not force a right-angle bend. For a crane, the hanging cable follows gravity while the boom has its own slope; compare their actual axes rather than the curved hook's outline.

For hinged screens and windows, estimate opening from visible construction, hinge and closed position. Diagonal_front is not a measurement of 45 degrees, side_profile does not imply 90 degrees between objects, and frontal versus side labels do not prove perpendicular physical axes. A ladder rising alongside a wall can be parallel to the wall even if seen from the side.

For a missing circular sector, trace the two cut boundaries back to their common center and estimate the wedge itself. Do not assume eight equal pizza slices merely because that is a familiar cutting pattern. For a shallow tray viewed exactly edge-on, the basic silhouette may be almost a line while its finite thickness forms a very thin profile; distinguish a basic outline description from an invented thick rectangle.

For a hypothetical side or top view, retain the particular object's curvature, openings, rim and protrusions. A dome-like canopy may have an approximately semicircular side outline despite seams and panels. A new viewpoint may also introduce occlusion by an overhanging branch; check the projected overlap instead of assuming every overhead object is transparent.

Use the named observer's eye location and body facing, not the camera origin, to decide which object is ahead or visible. For a seated person looking toward a window, compare the actual eye level with the point looked at; a window spanning that level can be straight ahead. A window or other architectural feature is not automatically above every seated person's gaze.

Locate what lies along the student's actual gaze ray and identify it by contents and structure. A glass-covered noticeboard is not necessarily a window merely because it is bright or glazed. Visible-to-camera and visible-to-a-seated-observer are different conditions; objects behind the observer or blocked along the eye line may be absent from their forward view.

Respect inward and outward relative to the interior of the doorway. An inward-opening door sweeps into the room, not automatically over an exterior step. Evaluate the dog's actual footprint separately from the door sweep rather than treating the entire step as blocked. For a sliding cabinet panel, inspect which opening the panel covers; do not treat objects on top as blocked solely because they share a side.

Directions such as front, left and backward may be relative to a truck or taxi. Moving in the vehicle's forward direction can appear as image left. Preserve that frame when mapping to the option text. For a route, follow successive connected segments and count every turn including entry into the requested parking area; do not infer a full sequence from just start and end positions.

An operation can require more than fitting inside a visible outline: placing a clock on a typewriter also requires a stable contact patch behind the keys. Separate whether temporary placement is possible from whether it remains upright. For climbing, compare actual slope, footholds and connection to the destination rather than assume all sides have equal difficulty.

When assessing evidence of handedness during polishing, inspect the repeated controlled wiping or manipulating action as well as the hand holding the object. Repetitive skilled action can reveal a consistent preferred active hand more clearly than a single pickup or put-down. Mere placement of an object to one side is not proof of the user's handedness.

Judge stability from the actual contact patch, center of mass, friction and support. A thin flexible packet standing on a narrow edge may depend on backing support; do not assume every sealed packet is a rigid freestanding box. Conversely, an unseen support remains a hypothesis unless the visible configuration requires it. A small gradual tilt need not immediately overcome friction or a local contact barrier.

Under shaking, mobility depends on contact geometry and resistance rather than flexibility alone. A smooth long cylinder can roll readily while a rough wound ball may deform and resist rolling; a stapler's broad flat base and a scissors' flat contact differ from cylindrical pencils. Do not claim all lighter or softer objects must move more.

For a point lamp and a fixed parallel receiving screen, shadow magnification equals light-to-screen distance divided by light-to-object distance. Moving the same object nearer the light can enlarge its projected shadow. For sunlight on level ground, shadow length instead depends on object height and solar elevation; do not apply a near-lamp rule universally to all ground shadows. Keep the light geometry specified in the question distinct from camera proximity.

Curved glass with water can produce reflection, refraction and multiple distorted images at once. Their apparent sizes depend on distances and curvature; do not assert a universal rule that one side's image shrinks whenever the other grows. Likewise a changing light's projected patch can be clipped into different shapes by an opening; the order of shapes must follow the stated motion and actual clipping geometry.

For nearest or farthest from a named object, first locate that reference and compare full relative positions, not just camera depth. Resolve multi-clause questions in sequence: identify the object a tool points toward, then apply the requested distance comparison to the correct referent. A missing reference cannot be assigned an invented coordinate.

Treat the cached scene graph and generated geometric deductions as fallible aids. Check actual image evidence when labels conflict with defining parts or relations. Evaluate the complete meaning of each option, keep physically valid conditions, and finish with a single selected option index rather than repeat speculative contradictions.
